claims.text: The thermal expansion behavior of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr differs as a function of temperature.
Differential thermal expansion among the constituent elements generates significant lattice distortion and residual thermal stress during cooling of HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual thermal stresses in HfNbTaTiZr alter dislocation mobility.
Residual thermal stress drives precipitation and hardening during aging of HfNbTaTiZr.
Precipitation and phase constitution can affect mechanical behavior in alloys derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system.
Temperature-dependent elastic behavior occurs in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
Residual thermal stress is responsible for changes in the elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr at intermediate temperatures.
Residual thermal stress hinders dislocation mobility and thereby enhances the high-temperature creep resistance of HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-expansion-induced residual stress provides a unified cause for the alloy's tensile-creep, cold-rolling microhardness, elastic-modulus, aging, and thermoelastic behavior.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr material is a homogeneous, single-phase BCC alloy with inherent lattice distortion.
Changing cooling rate or substrate thermal expansion coefficient will systematically vary residual thermal stress and lattice distortion in otherwise identical HfNbTaTiZr samples.
Samples with greater induced thermal mismatch and residual stress will have higher yield strength than samples cooled under baseline conditions.
Samples with greater induced thermal mismatch will exhibit altered elastic moduli.
Samples with greater induced thermal mismatch will exhibit slower creep rates at 1250 °C.
Hardening during aging at 600–800 °C will correlate with the level of pre-induced lattice distortion.
The proposed effects apply where diffusion is limited and secondary-phase formation remains minimal.
Evolution beyond a simple solid-solution state can cause significant deviations from the proposed behavior.

contradictions.description: The mechanism invokes precipitation and dynamic microstructural evolution as consequences of residual stress, whereas the boundary restricts the hypothesis to conditions with minimal secondary-phase formation.

The conditions include aging at 600–800 °C and creep at 1250 °C, while the boundary requires diffusion to remain limited; the hypothesis does not explain how that restriction is compatible with the high-temperature treatments.
